_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 590 words, six questions in text order: detail/opinion, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase, and a final question that links the ending back to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: The last time you'll hear it
subtitle: Wren Adeyemi records the sounds of Glasgow just before they disappear. Joe Marsh joined her for a very early start.

cards.text: Wren Adeyemi is standing in the middle of a car park in Glasgow at six o'clock on a Sunday morning, wearing enormous headphones and holding a microphone covered in grey fur. She looks, she cheerfully admits, 'like someone trying to catch a very small animal'. In fact she is recording a sound that will not exist next month: the creak and clatter of a ticket barrier that is about to be replaced by a silent automatic one. 'Everyone hates that barrier,' she says. 'It's slow and it sticks. But it's also the sound of this place, and nobody's going to miss it until it's gone.'
cards.question: What is Wren's opinion of the old ticket barrier?
choices: It should have been replaced years ago.
It is worth recording even though people dislike it.
It is the most interesting sound in the city.
It is too noisy for people who live nearby.
cards.highlight: But it's also the sound of this place, and nobody's going to miss it until it's gone.
cards.why: She accepts that 'everyone hates that barrier' but says 'it's also the sound of this place'. A is what other people feel, not her view, and she never compares it with other sounds in the city (C).

cards.text: Wren calls her project 'The Last Time', and over five years she has collected more than two thousand recordings. There is the final shift at a printing works, the bell of a school that has since closed, and an old lift in a department store that announced each floor in a voice from the 1970s. She began almost by accident, after her grandfather's corner shop was sold. 'I realised I could remember exactly what it looked like,' she says, 'but not what the door sounded like when it opened. I'd heard it a thousand times. And it was just gone.'
cards.question: What can we infer about how Wren's project started?
choices: She had always been interested in recording shops.
Her grandfather asked her to record his shop before it closed.
She was upset to find she had lost a sound she knew well.
She was given recording equipment by her grandfather.
cards.highlight: but not what the door sounded like when it opened
cards.why: She could remember how the shop looked 'but not what the door sounded like', though she had 'heard it a thousand times', and the project grew from that loss. Nothing says her grandfather asked her, so B is wrong.

cards.text: The hardest part of the job, surprisingly, is silence. A city is never truly quiet, and every recording picks up things Wren does not want: traffic, aeroplanes, people asking what she is doing. She once spent four nights trying to record a clock in a church tower and gave up every time because of a seagull that seemed to have chosen the same spot. 'It waited until the exact moment the clock struck,' she says, 'every single night.' In the end she kept the bird's cries in the recording. It is now one of her most popular.
cards.question: What does 'It' refer to in 'It waited until the exact moment the clock struck'?
choices: the seagull
the church tower
the clock
the recording
cards.highlight: because of a seagull that seemed to have chosen the same spot
cards.why: 'It' is the seagull mentioned just before, which made its noise exactly as the clock struck. The clock cannot wait for itself to strike, so C is wrong; the later 'It' refers to the recording.

cards.text: Her recordings are stored on a free website, arranged on a map of the city. Most listeners are local, but some of the warmest messages come from much further away. Last year a man in New Zealand wrote to say he had grown up above the printing works and had not heard its machines for forty years. He played the recording to his grandchildren, and then, he admitted, sat in the kitchen and cried. 'I nearly didn't record that place,' Wren says. 'It was too loud, the levels were all wrong. I'm so glad I didn't wait for perfect.'
cards.question: Why does the writer mention the man in New Zealand?
choices: to explain why Wren decided to make her website free
to show that recordings need to be technically perfect
to suggest that most of Wren's listeners live abroad
to show the effect the recordings can have on people far away
cards.highlight: He played the recording to his grandchildren, and then, he admitted, sat in the kitchen and cried.
cards.why: After forty years away, the man 'sat in the kitchen and cried', which shows how much a recording can mean. The text says 'most listeners are local', so C is wrong, and Wren is glad she 'didn't wait for perfect' (B).

cards.text: Not everyone understands the point. Wren has been asked by security guards to leave, by journalists whether she is 'against progress', and by her own mother when she is going to get a proper job. She does have one, in fact, part-time, editing sound for a radio station, which pays the bills. She insists, quite firmly, that she is not simply being nostalgic. 'I'm not saying the new barrier is worse,' she says. 'Honestly, it's probably better. I just want a record of what we had before. Somebody has to keep the receipts.'
cards.question: What does Wren mean by 'Somebody has to keep the receipts'?
choices: She is worried about how much her project costs.
Someone needs to keep evidence of how things used to be.
She would like to be paid for her recordings.
The city should not have spent money on a new barrier.
cards.highlight: I just want a record of what we had before.
cards.why: The 'receipts' are her recordings, proof of 'what we had before'. She says the new barrier is 'probably better', so she is not complaining about the money spent on it (D).

cards.text: By half past seven, the car park is beginning to fill up. A driver struggles with the barrier, which sticks, exactly as promised, and he swears at it loudly. Wren, still recording, gives me a delighted thumbs-up. Later, as we listen back in her van, I ask which sound she would most like to have recorded but missed. She thinks about it for a long time. 'My grandad's shop door,' she says eventually. Then she presses play, and the barrier creaks again, along with every word of the angry driver, saved now for anyone who cares to listen.
cards.question: What does the final paragraph suggest about Wren?
choices: She is annoyed that the driver spoiled her recording.
She has finally recorded her grandfather's shop door.
She values real everyday noise, including the unplanned parts.
She is thinking of giving up the project.
cards.highlight: Wren, still recording, gives me a delighted thumbs-up.
cards.why: The barrier from the opening sticks and the driver swears, and Wren gives 'a delighted thumbs-up', just as she kept the seagull. The shop door is the sound she 'missed', so B is wrong.
